366.text:
Schools, museums and television channels all use films to teach, and many people feel that documentary films are more educational than fictional films. I agree to a large extent, since documentaries present facts and evidence about real subjects, although fiction can teach in other ways.

To begin with, documentaries are usually more directly educational. They present facts, interviews and evidence about real subjects, such as wildlife, wars or scientific discoveries. A student who watches a documentary about the rainforest, for example, sees real animals, hears from biologists and learns how forests affect the climate, all within one hour. Maps, graphs and archive film make complex information clear, and the viewer can check the sources and continue reading afterwards. Teachers often use documentaries to supplement textbooks, because they bring distant places and events into the classroom. Because they aim to inform, they usually stay close to the truth and avoid the invented events and exaggerations that fiction often contains.

However, fiction can also teach important lessons. Stories build understanding of people and history through characters who move viewers, and they develop empathy by letting audiences see the world through other eyes. A film about a family during a war, for example, may help young people to understand suffering far better than a list of dates and numbers. Historical dramas can inspire interest in a period that leads viewers to further study. Both belong in education, but they serve different purposes: documentaries give knowledge and evidence, and fiction gives emotional insight. Teachers should combine them and encourage students to ask which parts are true and which are imagined.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that documentary films are more educational than fictional films, although fiction has its own value.

Largely agree; hư cấu có giá trị riêng.

377.text:
Children see thousands of advertisements every year, and some believe that advertising to children should be tightly regulated. I agree to a large extent, since children cannot judge persuasion and need protection, although parents also have a role.

To begin with, advertising to children should be tightly regulated because they are unable to judge persuasion. Young children do not understand that adverts sell, so cartoon characters and games lead them to demand toys and sugary snacks. A boy who sees a famous footballer promoting a fizzy drink, for example, may believe that the drink will make him strong, and he will ask his parents for it repeatedly. Advertisers deliberately use bright colours, catchy songs and free gifts to attract children and to create brand loyalty at an early age. This pressure on parents, called pester power, causes family conflict and spending that families may not be able to afford, and it increases demand for unhealthy products.

However, regulation should be balanced and supported by other measures. Parents have an important responsibility to monitor what their children watch, to explain how advertising works and to say no. Schools can include media education in their lessons, and broadcasters can voluntarily follow codes of conduct. Some advertisements for books, sports equipment or educational products are beneficial, so a total ban may be unnecessary. Strict rules should nevertheless exist: governments can prohibit adverts for unhealthy foods during children's programmes, forbid the use of cartoon characters to sell harmful products, ban direct appeals to buy and check that websites and games do not hide promotions in entertainment. Effective enforcement with fines for violations is essential.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising to children should be tightly regulated, as long as parents and schools also help children to understand advertising.

386.text:
Followers see influencers on tropical beaches, in luxury hotels and in spotless homes, and many feel that influencer culture creates unrealistic lifestyles. I agree with this view, since sponsored, staged and edited content hides the effort and money behind it.

To begin with, influencer culture creates unrealistic lifestyles by showing sponsored, staged and edited versions of life. Free gifts, paid trips and perfect scenes hide the effort and money behind them. A travel influencer who posts a photograph from a luxury resort, for example, may have received the stay free in return for promotion, and may have taken dozens of shots before choosing the one with perfect light. The viewer, who sees only the final picture, believes that the lifestyle is normal and affordable. Many influencers rent clothes, cars and even houses for filming, and some use filters that change their appearance. The constant stream of glamorous images makes ordinary routines look dull by comparison.

Furthermore, this affects followers. People feel that their own lives are not good enough, and some spend money or borrow to keep up with what they see. Young people, who spend hours on these platforms, are particularly vulnerable, and studies connect heavy use with anxiety and low self-confidence. However, not every influencer is dishonest, and some share real struggles and everyday life. Honest disclosure and critical viewing reduce the harm. Rules can require influencers to label paid partnerships and edited images, and platforms can promote creators who show realistic content. Parents and teachers should discuss with young people how these images are produced and encourage them to measure their lives by their own values.

In conclusion, I agree that influencer culture creates unrealistic lifestyles, but transparency and media education can reduce its effects.

414.text:
False health advice, doctored photographs and invented political stories circulate widely, and opinions differ on whether individuals should be responsible for reporting misinformation or whether society and government should act. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that ordinary users are best placed to notice and report false posts. Users spot false posts quickly and can report them. A teacher who sees a fake claim about a vaccine in a parents' group, for example, can flag it and explain the facts before it spreads, and thousands of such reports can help platforms to find harmful material. People who check a source before sharing, and who correct friends politely, make it more difficult for rumours to travel. Since misinformation spreads through personal networks, personal habits are important, and a population that learns to think critically is the strongest defence.

On the other hand, advocates of action by society and government point out that individuals lack the power to remove false posts, to check facts at scale or to punish deliberate spreaders. Individuals can flag misinformation but platforms and governments must act on it. Companies decide how algorithms work and can slow the spread of false stories, fact-checking organisations need funding, and laws can penalise organised campaigns that aim to deceive voters. A single user cannot stop a network of fake accounts, for example, that floods a platform with false claims. Without official action, reports are often ignored.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that responsibility is shared: individuals should check and report misleading content, while platforms and governments must act on reports and enforce clear rules against deliberate disinformation.

426.text:
Every evening, millions of people switch on the television to follow news from their country and the world, and many feel that television news is biased. I agree to a large extent, since ownership, selection and sensationalism shape the reports, although regulations limit the worst bias.

To begin with, television news is often biased through ownership, selection and sensationalism. Owners and advertisers influence what is covered, editors choose dramatic stories, and presenters frame events. A channel owned by a political party, for example, may report the successes of its allies at length and mention the failures of opponents only briefly. Even when no one intends to deceive, the choice of which stories to show and which to leave out affects what viewers think is important. Violent and emotional items attract audiences, so crime and conflict receive more time than calm progress. Short bulletins also encourage simple explanations of complex issues, and the choice of images, words and guests can lead viewers toward one conclusion.

However, bias is not complete, and professional codes and regulators limit the worst cases. Many channels follow rules about accuracy and fairness, correct mistakes and give opponents the right to reply, and public broadcasters are required to be balanced. Journalists often try sincerely to present several sides. A report that shows both a government plan and the criticism of it, for example, helps viewers to form their own opinions. The sensible response is for viewers to compare several sources, including newspapers, radio and reliable websites, and to ask who owns a channel and what interests it may have. Schools can teach this critical approach.

In conclusion, I agree to a large extent that television news is biased, but comparing sources and strong rules can limit its influence.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: tin tức truyền hình thiên lệch — largely agree

plan.think: Mở bài nêu hàng triệu người bật tivi xem tin; largely agree.

Thiên lệch qua chủ sở hữu, chọn lọc, giật gân: chủ và nhà quảng cáo ảnh hưởng, biên tập chọn câu chuyện kịch tính, người dẫn đóng khung; ví dụ kênh của đảng chính trị đưa thành công đồng minh dài, thất bại đối thủ ngắn; không cố ý vẫn ảnh hưởng điều coi là quan trọng; bạo lực, cảm xúc hút khán giả; bản tin ngắn đơn giản hoá; hình ảnh, từ ngữ, khách mời dẫn đến một kết luận.

Không hoàn toàn: quy tắc nghề, cơ quan quản lý; chính xác, công bằng, đính chính, quyền phản hồi; đài công cân bằng; nhà báo cố gắng trình bày nhiều mặt; ví dụ báo cáo cho cả kế hoạch chính phủ và chỉ trích giúp hình thành ý kiến; so sánh nhiều nguồn, hỏi chủ sở hữu; trường dạy.
Largely agree; so sánh nguồn và quy định mạnh hạn chế.

465.text:
In many villages and remote districts, the internet is slow, newspapers arrive late and television reception is poor, and this essay will discuss the role of community radio in rural areas, focusing on information and on community voice.

To begin with, community radio gives rural people information and education where other media are scarce. It broadcasts farming advice, weather warnings and health messages in local languages, costs little to receive and can be heard on a cheap battery set. A farmer who hears a daily programme about prices at the market, for example, can decide when to sell his harvest, and a mother who listens to a health talk learns how to prevent common diseases in children. During floods, storms or epidemics, stations can issue immediate warnings and instructions, which saves lives. Programmes can also support adult literacy and school lessons for children who live far from classrooms.

Furthermore, community radio gives rural people a voice and strengthens identity. Local volunteers present programmes, so the content reflects the language, music and concerns of the community, and residents can phone in to discuss problems with officials. Stories, songs and traditions are recorded and preserved, and young people gain experience in broadcasting. In places with many languages, minority groups can hear their own speech on air. However, stations often lack money, equipment and trained staff, and may face political pressure. Governments and donors can help by providing low-cost licences, training and funds, and by guaranteeing editorial independence. Rural communities then become better informed and more united.

In conclusion, community radio plays an essential role in rural areas by providing useful information and giving local people a voice, and it deserves support.

analysis.type_vi: Opinion: vai trò đài cộng đồng ở nông thôn

plan.think: Mở bài nêu làng xa internet chậm, báo đến muộn; hai ý: thông tin; tiếng nói cộng đồng.

Thông tin, giáo dục nơi phương tiện khác khan hiếm: tư vấn nông nghiệp, cảnh báo thời tiết, thông điệp y tế bằng tiếng địa phương, rẻ, đài pin; ví dụ nông dân nghe chương trình giá chợ quyết định bán mùa, bà mẹ nghe nói chuyện sức khoẻ phòng bệnh trẻ; lũ, bão, dịch cảnh báo tức thì cứu mạng; xoá mù chữ, bài học cho trẻ ở xa lớp.

Tiếng nói và bản sắc: tình nguyện viên địa phương dẫn nên nội dung phản ánh ngôn ngữ, âm nhạc, mối quan tâm; gọi vào thảo luận với quan chức; ghi truyện, bài hát, truyền thống; người trẻ học phát thanh; nhóm thiểu số nghe tiếng mình; nhưng thiếu tiền, thiết bị, nhân viên, áp lực chính trị; giấy phép rẻ, đào tạo, quỹ, độc lập biên tập.
Vai trò thiết yếu, xứng đáng hỗ trợ.

466.text:
Millions of viewers watch talent shows in which famous singers, dancers and producers decide who goes through to the next round, and many feel that celebrity judges on talent shows are unfair. I agree to some extent, since entertainment value and personal taste can outweigh talent, although many judges give honest and useful feedback.

To begin with, celebrity judges can be unfair when entertainment value and personal taste outweigh talent. Producers want drama, so judges may mock contestants or favour characters with a good story. A shy singer with a beautiful voice, for example, may be criticised harshly or sent home, while a less talented contestant who is funny or emotional receives praise because he makes better television. Judges may have favourites from the beginning, and their comments may follow a script written to create conflict. Some contestants have said that they were chosen or rejected according to the story the programme wanted to tell. Because judges are celebrities themselves, they may also be tempted to say shocking things in order to attract attention.

However, many judges are experienced professionals, whose honest feedback helps performers to improve. A well-known vocal coach who tells a candidate that her pitch is unreliable, for example, gives advice that may help her for years. The judging of art is also partly subjective, so differences in opinion are natural and do not always indicate unfairness. Transparent voting and fair rules improve trust. Many shows now give the audience a vote, publish the criteria for judging and use independent supervisors to check procedures. Contestants should also be given clear contracts that explain how the programme will edit and present them.

In conclusion, I agree to some extent that celebrity judges can be unfair, but transparency and public voting can make talent shows fairer.

analysis.type_vi: Agree/Disagree: giám khảo nổi tiếng trên chương trình tài năng không công bằng — agree một phần

plan.think: Mở bài nêu chương trình tài năng với giám khảo nổi tiếng; agree một phần.

Không công bằng khi giá trị giải trí, sở thích cá nhân hơn tài năng: nhà sản xuất muốn kịch tính, giám khảo chế giễu hoặc thiên vị nhân vật có câu chuyện; ví dụ ca sĩ nhút nhát giọng đẹp bị chê, về, thí sinh kém hơn hài hước, xúc động được khen vì hay trên tivi; có người yêu thích từ đầu; bình luận theo kịch bản gây xung đột; thí sinh nói bị chọn, loại theo câu chuyện; giám khảo nổi tiếng nói gây sốc.

Nhiều giám khảo chuyên nghiệp, phản hồi trung thực giúp; ví dụ huấn luyện viên thanh nhạc nói cao độ không ổn cho lời khuyên nhiều năm; đánh giá nghệ thuật phần chủ quan; bình chọn minh bạch, quy tắc công bằng: khán giả bình chọn, công bố tiêu chí, người giám sát độc lập; hợp đồng rõ ràng cho thí sinh.
Agree một phần; minh bạch và bình chọn công khai làm công bằng hơn.

500.text:
Many people check platforms such as Facebook or Instagram several times a day, while others prefer meetings, phone calls or hobbies, and opinions differ on whether social media or alternatives are better. This essay will consider both views before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of social media argue that it is convenient for staying in touch. Platforms connect many people instantly, whatever the distance. A student who studies abroad, for example, can see her family's photographs and send a message in seconds, and she can follow news and join groups that match her interests. Social media also helps small businesses to find customers, allows people to share ideas and organise events, and gives a voice to those who might not be heard otherwise. It is usually free, and users can choose when to respond, which suits busy schedules.

On the other hand, supporters of alternatives argue that they give deeper relationships. Platforms distract and reduce privacy, whereas face-to-face contact, phone calls and hobbies offer fuller attention and trust. A group of friends who meet every week to play football or to cook together, for example, build stronger bonds than those who only exchange comments online. Voice and video calls convey emotion more clearly than text, and offline hobbies such as reading, music or sport improve concentration and health. Social media can also encourage comparison, anxiety and wasted time, so some people deliberately reduce their use. A mix suits most people.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that social media is useful for keeping in contact and sharing information, but it should supplement and not replace meetings, calls and offline activities.

analysis.type_vi: Discuss both views: mạng xã hội hay lựa chọn khác

plan.think: Mở bài nêu người kiểm tra nền tảng nhiều lần mỗi ngày, người khác ưa gặp, gọi, sở thích.

Tiện giữ liên lạc: kết nối tức thì bất kể khoảng cách; ví dụ sinh viên học nước ngoài xem ảnh gia đình, gửi tin trong vài giây, theo dõi tin, nhóm sở thích; doanh nghiệp nhỏ tìm khách, chia sẻ ý tưởng, tổ chức sự kiện, tiếng nói người ít được nghe; miễn phí, chọn lúc phản hồi.

Quan hệ sâu hơn: nền tảng xao nhãng, giảm riêng tư; gặp trực tiếp, gọi, sở thích chú ý và tin tưởng đầy đủ; ví dụ nhóm bạn gặp mỗi tuần đá bóng hay nấu ăn gắn bó hơn bình luận trực tuyến; gọi thoại, video truyền cảm xúc rõ hơn; sở thích ngoại tuyến cải thiện tập trung, sức khoẻ; mạng xã hội gây so sánh, lo âu, mất thời gian; kết hợp.
Mạng xã hội bổ sung chứ không thay thế.
